title: Testing the Thermomix TM7 for a Month: Worth $1,600?
creator: Grace Whitfield
description:
I cooked almost every dinner for a month in the Thermomix TM7. Bread, risotto, curries, and one tragic custard. Is it worth that price, or is it a very expensive blender?

I bought this machine myself through a local consultant. Nobody from the company has seen this video.

Recipes I made are listed in the pinned comment.

sentences.t: Right, this is the Thermomix TM7, and it cost me just over sixteen hundred dollars.
I know, I know.
I've wanted one for years, and I finally gave in, so I'm going to tell you whether that was a terrible decision.
First, how do you even buy one, because it's a bit strange.
You can't just walk into a shop and pick up a Thermomix, you buy it through a consultant, who comes to your house and does a cooking demo.
Mine was a lovely woman called Sandra, she made us a soup and a sorbet in about twenty minutes, and then she sold me a Thermomix.
The TM7 comes with a trial of Cookidoo, which is the recipe platform, and after that it's a yearly subscription if you want the guided recipes.
And that's honestly my biggest gripe with the Thermomix, because the machine is great, but a lot of the magic lives behind that subscription.
Without Cookidoo the Thermomix still works, you can set temperature, speed and time manually, but it's a lot less hand-holdy.
Okay, week one.
I started easy, with a mushroom risotto.
If you've ever made risotto, you know it's twenty-five minutes of standing there stirring.
Here, you put everything in, press go, and it stirs for you.
And it was really good, creamy, properly cooked, I was genuinely impressed.
My partner said it was better than mine, which I will never forgive him for.
Week two was bread.
It kneads the dough for you, which is nice, but you still need an oven, obviously.
The first loaf came out dense, because I followed the recipe exactly and my kitchen is cold.
Second loaf, I let it rise longer, and it was much better.
So it doesn't replace knowing how to cook, it just takes some of the boring bits off your hands.
Week three, I tried to break it.
Curry paste from scratch, which normally means a lot of pounding in a mortar.
It made a smooth paste in about thirty seconds.
Nut butter, also fine, though the motor got loud and a bit warm.
And then custard.
Oh, the custard.
I skipped a step on the guided recipe because I thought I knew better, and it split into sweet scrambled eggs.
That one's on me, not the machine.
Now, the downsides.
The bowl isn't huge, so for a family of five or six you'll be cooking in two batches.
Cleaning is okay, the bowl goes in the dishwasher, but the blade bit is fiddly and sharp.
And the price, I mean, I keep coming back to it.
For the same money you could buy a good stand mixer, a blender, a slow cooker and a decent knife, and still have money left over.
So is it worth it?
If you hate cooking and you've got the money, it'll probably change how often you cook at home.
If you already love cooking, I think you'll find it useful but not life-changing.
For me, I'm keeping it, mostly for risotto and soups, and I'll check back in six months to see if it's living on the counter or in the cupboard.
Thanks for watching, and let me know if there's anything you want me to throw in it.
